production_notes: [VERIFY] content.md's statement that clients and employers increasingly ask how work was made is left out of the voiceover. The script says only that vague AI claims are not useful and that hiding AI use can damage trust.

[REGION] Trademark clearance and rules on publishing research or client material differ by country; the script asks learners not to claim legal results they do not have ('trademark search recommended', not 'trademark cleared').

Native-speaker check needed: the Yoruba meaning check in the worked example (two rejected names with negative meanings in Yoruba) is hypothetical. The rejected names are not shown or spoken. Before recording, confirm with a native Yoruba speaker that 'Tidewell' has no unwanted meaning, and do not invent Yoruba words for the slide.
'Tidewell' and Fatima Bello's water delivery brand are fictional. Scene 12 says the rejected blue looked close to 'many existing water brands': do not show or name any real water brand.
This is the final lesson: the CTA congratulates learners and points to the capstone submission and rubric (capstone_rubric.md).

Hook.voiceover: Two designers show the same polished app. One says, I used AI. The other shows exactly where AI helped, where she overruled it, and which risks she checked. Which one would you hire?

Explain.voiceover: This is the final lesson. Last time, you critiqued your work and built an asset log. Now you tell the story, in the capstone: writing the AI-assisted design case study.

slide.title: Capstone: Writing the AI-Assisted Design Case Study
slide.body: AI for Brand and Product Design · Lesson 14 of 14 · Capstone step 5

Explain.voiceover: Your capstone is a brand identity and a key app screen flow, designed with an AI-assisted process, and documented as a case study. You have already built most of it. Guidelines in lesson ten. Screens in lesson eleven. The prototype in lesson twelve. And the checklist and asset log in lesson thirteen.

slide.title: You have built most of it
slide.body: Four tiles feeding into one 'Case study' box: Guidelines (L10) · Screens (L11) · Prototype (L12) · Checklist and asset log (L13)

Explain.voiceover: A case study is not a gallery. It shows how you think. Use five sections. Problem: the client, the audience, the goal and one success measure. Process: the main stages, with drafts and dead ends, not only the final result. And an AI use log: where you used AI, what you kept, and what you changed or rejected.

slide.title: The case study template, 1 to 3
slide.body: 1. Problem: client, audience, goal, one success measure · 2. Process: main stages, drafts and dead ends · 3. AI use log: stage, tool, asked for, kept, changed or rejected

Explain.voiceover: Include at least one case where you overruled AI, and why. Then Decisions: the three to five most important design and risk decisions, with reasons. And finally Outcomes: the final brand and flow, a link to the prototype, what your test found, and what you learned.

slide.title: The case study template, 4 and 5
slide.body: At least one 'overruled AI' case · 4. Decisions: 3 to 5 design and risk decisions, with reasons · 5. Outcomes: final brand and flow, prototype link, test findings, lessons learned

Explain.voiceover: Be honest and specific about AI. A vague phrase like AI-powered design is not useful, and hiding AI use can damage trust. A specific sentence is useful. For example: Claude grouped anonymised interview notes into themes, I verified every quote, and I removed one theme.

slide.title: Vague or specific?
slide.body: Red cross: 'AI-powered design.' Green tick: 'Claude grouped anonymised interview notes into themes; I verified every quote and removed one theme.'

Explain.voiceover: And never claim a legal result you did not get. Write trademark search recommended, not trademark cleared. Protect data here too. Use anonymised research, and publish client details only with approval.

Think of a case study as a cooking programme, not a restaurant photo. The photo shows the dish. The programme shows the ingredients, the steps, the mistakes and the choices. So the viewer trusts that the cook can do it again.
Explain.stock_query: chef cooking on camera in studio kitchen
Explain.on_screen_text: A cooking programme, not a photo

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's look at an example. Fatima Bello is a brand and product designer in Lagos, Nigeria. For her capstone, she creates a fictional drinking-water delivery brand for apartment buildings. She uses everything from this course.
Demonstrate.stock_query: water bottle delivery to apartment building

Demonstrate.voiceover: Her AI use log is a clear table. In research, Claude found themes, and she removed one theme with a changed quote. In naming, she shortlisted Tidewell, and rejected two names with negative meanings in Yoruba. From her moodboards, she removed images with text artefacts.

slide.title: Fatima's AI use log, part 1
slide.body: Research · Claude · themes from 10 anonymised notes · kept 4 · removed 1 with a changed quote. Naming · Claude · 20 names in 4 categories · 'Tidewell' shortlisted · rejected 2 names with negative meanings in Yoruba. Moodboards · image generator · Direction B · removed images with text artefacts.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Her logo concepts came from an image generator, but the final mark is a full vector redraw, with no traced shapes. The UI draft from Figma was rebuilt with components. And she rejected an error message that blamed the user.

slide.title: Fatima's AI use log, part 2
slide.body: Logo · image generator, Figma · wave-and-drop idea · full vector redraw, no traced shapes. UI · Figma AI features · layout structure · rebuilt with components, contrast fixed. Microcopy · Claude · 3 lines edited · rejected a message that blamed the user.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Her decisions section explains why she overruled Claude's bright blue palette. Two text pairs failed contrast, and the colour looked too close to many existing water brands.

slide.title: Overruled: the bright blue
slide.body: Claude's bright blue palette (red cross): two text pairs fail contrast · too close to many existing water brands. Fatima's final palette (green tick). No real brands shown.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Her outcomes section links the prototype. Her tester could not find the delivery time, so she moved it to the confirm screen. One small test, one clear improvement. And the asset log shows the logo as needs check, with a trademark search recommended.

slide.title: Outcomes
slide.body: Prototype link · Test finding: delivery time hard to find → moved to the confirm screen · Asset log row: Logo, 'Needs check: trademark search recommended'

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to write only about the final visuals, or to list AI tools without saying what they did. Both hide your judgement, and your judgement is the most valuable part. Show the process, including the moments when you rejected AI output.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Show your judgement, not just visuals.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, structure your case study as problem, process, AI use log, decisions and outcomes. Second, be honest and specific about AI use, including where you overruled it, and never claim legal clearance you do not have. Third, protect data in the case study, with anonymised research, and client details only with approval.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Problem · Process · AI use log · Decisions · Outcomes. 2. Honest, specific AI use; no claimed legal clearance. 3. Anonymised research; client details only with approval.

CTA.voiceover: Congratulations. You have completed AI for Brand and Product Design. For the last step of your capstone, write and lay out your case study in Figma, covering your brand identity, your key screen flow and your AI-assisted process. It takes about sixty minutes. Check it against the rubric, and then submit it. You have learned to use AI with craft and control. Well done, and good luck.
